propositions.text: Once the Crown establishes certain conditions, the accused must raise a reasonable doubt about breathalyzer test reliability.
propositions.quote: the burden shifts to the accused to raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the breathalyzer test results.

propositions.text: If no evidence raises doubt, the results are presumed accurate, reflecting the blood alcohol level at testing and at the material time.
propositions.quote: the results are presumed to be accurate, which is to say that the alcohol level in the breath sample is presumed to reflect the alcohol level in the accused’s blood at the time of testing, and that level is presumed to be identical to the alcohol level in the accused’s blood at the material time.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown must prove certain conditions; the accused must then raise a doubt about test reliability, which, if not done, results are presumed accurate.

propositions.text: This appeal concerns the scope of evidence needed to rebut presumptions of breathalyzer test accuracy and identity.
propositions.quote: This appeal concerns the scope of the evidence that must be adduced to rebut the presumptions of accuracy and identity that are applicable to breathalyzer test results under s. 258(1) (c) of the Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C‑46 (“Cr. C.”).

propositions.text: The Court allowed the Crown’s appeal, set aside the acquittal, and ordered a new trial.
propositions.quote: from the bench, the Court allowed the Crown’s appeal from the judgment of the Court of Appeal, set aside the verdict of acquittal restored by the Court of Appeal, and ordered a new trial, with reasons to follow.

propositions.text: This decision follows the Court’s review of the scope of evidence needed to rebut presumptions under s. 258(1)(c).
propositions.quote: These are those reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The appeal concerns the evidence required to rebut presumptions of breathalyzer test reliability, with the Court ordering a new trial.

propositions.text: The extent of the burden on an accused has been settled in R. v. St‑Onge Lamoureux, 2012 SCC 57.
propositions.quote: In R. v. St‑Onge Lamoureux, 2012 SCC 57, [2012] 3 S.C.R. 187, this Court put an end to that debate.

propositions.text: To rebut the presumption, evidence must show malfunction or improper operation of the instrument casts doubt on reliability.
propositions.quote: the new provisions [of the Cr. C.] do not make it impossible to disprove the test results. Rather, Parliament has recognized that the results will be reliable only if the instruments are operated and maintained properly, and that there might be deficiencies in the maintenance of the instruments or in the test process. What the new provisions require is that evidence tending to cast doubt on the reliability of the results relate directly to such deficiencies.

propositions.text: Evidence must relate directly to deficiencies in operation or maintenance to rebut the presumption.
propositions.quote: What the new provisions require is that evidence tending to cast doubt on the reliability of the results relate directly to such deficiencies.

propositions.text: The evidence must establish that the defect could have affected the results’ reliability.
propositions.quote: the evidence must establish that, in the particular case, the defect could have affected the reliability of the results.

paragraphs.summary: The Court clarifies that evidence must relate directly to instrument deficiencies and could have affected results to rebut the presumption.

propositions.text: The accused’s burden is discharged if evidence shows a defect in operation that could affect reliability.
propositions.quote: The accused’s burden is discharged if the following conditions are met: (i) the accused adduces evidence relating directly to the malfunctioning or improper operation of the instrument, and (ii) the accused establishes that this defect tends to cast doubt on the reliability of the results.

propositions.text: The defect must be linked to a specific procedure and shown to have affected the results.
propositions.quote: the defect could have affected the reliability of the results. The evidence from which it can be inferred that the defect tends to cast doubt on the reliability of the results must be looked at in the same manner. The theoretical element is satisfied where it is proved that the purpose of the procedure in question is to ensure the reliability of the results. On the practical element, the evidence must establish that, in the particular case, the defect could have affected the reliability of the results.

paragraphs.summary: The burden is met if evidence shows a defect related to a procedure that could have affected the results’ reliability.

propositions.text: No need to address the first condition; no evidence that improper operation cast doubt on reliability.
propositions.quote: In the instant case, there is no need to deal with the first condition. Even if we assume, without deciding, that improper operation of the instrument was established here based on failure to complete the 15‑ or 20‑minute observation period, there was clearly no evidence that this improper operation tended to cast doubt on the reliability of the results.

propositions.text: The Court of Appeal’s judgment is reversed; the Superior Court’s order for a new trial is restored.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal’s judgment must be reversed. The Superior Court’s judgment setting aside the verdict of acquittal by the Court of Québec and ordering a new trial must be restored.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds no evidence that improper operation affected reliability, reversing the Court of Appeal and restoring the Superior Court’s order.

propositions.text: On July 12, 2012, the respondent was stopped and arrested, then taken to the police station.
propositions.quote: On July 12, 2012, the respondent Marc Cyr‑Langlois was stopped by Constables Boissonneault and Cousineau while he was driving his vehicle.

propositions.text: Constable Boissonneault prepared the instrument and ran a control test; Constable Cousineau observed the respondent and called his counsel.
propositions.quote: Constable Boissonneault, a qualified technician, went into the breathalyzer room to prepare the instrument and run a control test. Constable Cousineau accompanied the respondent to the interrogation room and then joined Constable Boissonneault in the adjacent breathalyzer room while the respondent exercised his right to counsel confidentially.

propositions.text: The respondent was tested twice, with results over the legal limit, leading to charges.
propositions.quote: At 1:08 a.m., Constable Boissonneault gave the respondent a first breathalyzer test, which showed 157 mg of alcohol in 100 ml of blood. During the statutory waiting period prior to the second test, the respondent was alone with Constable Cousineau in the interrogation room. At 1:30 a.m., Constable Boissonneault administered the second breathalyzer test, which showed 148 mg of alcohol in 100 ml of blood.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent was stopped, tested twice with results over the limit, and charged; police procedures and timing are detailed.

propositions.text: In the Court of Québec, the issue was whether the technician breached duty by not observing the accused for 15-20 minutes.
propositions.quote: At trial in the Court of Québec, the parties agreed that the court should begin by determining whether Constable Boissonneault had breached the duty to operate the breathalyzer properly by failing to observe the accused himself for a period of 15 or 20 minutes before administering each test.

propositions.text: The accused argued that such a breach would rebut the presumption, leading to acquittal.
propositions.quote: The accused argued that, in such a case, the presumptions were rebutted, which had to lead to his acquittal in the absence of additional evidence from the Crown.

propositions.text: The trial judge found the procedure was not properly followed, leading to an acquittal.
propositions.quote: He then stated that, since the general purpose of the observation procedure is to ensure the reliability of the results, his finding that the procedure had not been followed in this case was sufficient to raise a reasonable doubt. He did not refer to any additional evidence in this regard. He therefore acquitted the respondent of the second charge.

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Québec considered whether breach of observation procedure rebutted the presumption, leading to acquittal based on doubt.

propositions.text: The Crown appealed, arguing the trial judge erred in law by acquitting the respondent.
propositions.quote: Since it was of the view that the evidence required to rebut the presumptions had not been adduced, the Crown appealed as of right to the Superior Court, which allowed the appeal, set aside the judgment of acquittal and ordered a new trial.

propositions.text: The Superior Court found the trial judge erred in law and ordered a new trial.
propositions.quote: Zigman J. relied on the principles enunciated in R. v. So, 2014 ABCA 451, 9 Alta. L.R. (6th) 382, and concluded as follows: The Court agrees with the principles stated by the Alberta Court of Appeal at paragraph 47 of So, and it therefore concludes that in this case, the trial judge did not properly apply the law and made a fatal error of law in acquitting the [respondent].

paragraphs.summary: The Crown appealed the acquittal, and the Superior Court found legal error, ordering a new trial.

propositions.text: The Alberta Court of Appeal summarized the burden of proof for rebutting presumptions.
propositions.quote: In So, the Alberta Court of Appeal had summarized the burden of proof that rests on an accused in such circumstances as follows: To rebut the statutory presumptions an accused must establish to the reasonable doubt standard: (a) a deficiency in the functioning or operation of the instrument; and (b) that the deficiency directly related to the reliability of the breath test results.

propositions.text: The Court of Appeal set aside the Superior Court’s judgment and restored the acquittal.
propositions.quote: A majority of the Court of Appeal set aside the Superior Court’s judgment and restored the verdict of acquittal.

propositions.text: The majority required evidence that the defect could influence the results.
propositions.quote: All of the judges agreed that an accused must not only establish that the breathalyzer was operated improperly, but must also adduce evidence tending to show that its improper operation [translation] “[could] influence the result” (paras. 38 and 69 (CanLII)).

propositions.text: The dissent believed the trial judge was correct in not finding a defect that could affect the result.
propositions.quote: The dissenting judge would have upheld the Superior Court’s decision on the ground that “[t]he [Court of Québec] judge was not faced with evidence showing a deficiency [that could] affect the result”.

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal required evidence that a defect could influence results; dissenting judge disagreed with this standard.

propositions.text: The key issue is how an accused can show a defect tends to cast doubt on reliability when there is evidence of improper operation.
propositions.quote: The only real issue is how, in cases where there is evidence that an instrument was operated improperly (the respondent not having challenged the functioning of the instrument), the accused can show that this defect tends to cast doubt on the reliability of the results.

propositions.text: Is purely theoretical evidence sufficient to raise a reasonable doubt?
propositions.quote: The heart of the dispute comes down to the following: is evidence that is purely theoretical sufficient for this purpose?

paragraphs.summary: The main issue is whether theoretical evidence alone can raise a reasonable doubt about test reliability.

propositions.text: Concrete, fact-related evidence is more likely to meet the requirement than abstract evidence.
propositions.quote: While it is not impossible that abstract evidence alone may sometimes meet the requirement of raising a reasonable doubt about the reliability of results, it is more likely that evidence that relates more concretely to the facts in issue will be required.

propositions.text: Without such evidence, the argument is speculative and cannot satisfy the reasonable doubt standard.
propositions.quote: without such evidence, the accused’s argument was in the realm of speculation and could not satisfy the reasonable doubt test (St‑Onge Lamoureux, at paras. 52‑53).

paragraphs.summary: Concrete, fact-related evidence is generally required; speculation does not meet the reasonable doubt standard.

propositions.text: Relying on mere hypothetical evidence is insufficient to raise a reasonable doubt.
propositions.quote: Relying on such evidence amounts to accepting a [translation] “mere hypothetical possibility”, which is clearly not sufficient to raise a reasonable doubt (R. v. Lifchus, [1997] 3 S.C.R. 320, at para. 30).

propositions.text: The evidence must be concrete and show that the defect could have affected the results.
propositions.quote: the minimum evidence required for this purpose was simply not adduced.

paragraphs.summary: Hypothetical evidence is insufficient; concrete evidence is needed to show a defect could affect results.

propositions.text: Improper operation may be so serious that it alone can raise a reasonable doubt.
propositions.quote: I do not rule out the possibility that improper operation may be so serious or so closely connected with reliability that it will be sufficient in itself to raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the results obtained.

propositions.text: The seriousness of the defect must be enough to raise a reasonable doubt, regardless of how it is inferred.
propositions.quote: What is essential is that the possibility that the defect affected the reliability of the results is serious enough to raise a reasonable doubt.

propositions.text: Expert evidence is not essential; concrete evidence must link the defect to the results.
propositions.quote: Although expert evidence is not essential, concrete evidence must be tendered to show that the improper operation or malfunctioning of the instrument may be linked to the results.

propositions.text: The evidence should not be mere hypothesis or conjecture.
propositions.quote: In sum, the evidence should not be mere hypothesis or conjecture.

paragraphs.summary: Serious defects may alone raise doubt; evidence must be concrete, not conjecture, to link defect to results.

propositions.text: An intervener argues that testifying about digestive issues might contravene s. 258(1) (d.01) Cr. C.
propositions.quote: An intervener, the Criminal Lawyers’ Association, argues that it would be impossible for an accused to testify about his or her alcohol consumption or digestive problems without contravening s. 258(1) (d.01) Cr. C.

propositions.text: The Court clarifies that issues related to proper functioning are different from issues about the defendant’s health.
propositions.quote: It is well established that challenges to the presumptions in s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C. can be based only on issues relating to the proper functioning and proper operation of an instrument. However, an accused who testifies to establish that he or she had a digestive problem is not seeking thereby to show that the instrument was operated improperly.

propositions.text: Testifying about health issues is admissible and does not necessarily violate the law.
propositions.quote: the fact that such testimonial evidence is admissible does not make it compulsory.

paragraphs.summary: Testifying about health issues like digestion is different from challenging instrument operation; it is admissible.

propositions.text: The respondent claims he did not present a “burping defence,” but it was central to his argument.
propositions.quote: The burping defence was an essential part of his arguments. He argued that the improper operation of the instrument cast doubt on the reliability of the results precisely because, in such a case, the police might not notice certain digestive issues that can have a distorting effect.

propositions.text: The central issue was whether the defect could affect the results’ reliability.
propositions.quote: the discussion during the hearing before the Court of Québec judge confirms that this question was central to the respondent’s submissions.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent’s argument centered on whether digestive issues could affect test reliability, constituting a “burping defence.”

propositions.text: There was no evidence that the defect affected the results, so the defect could not form the basis of a reasonable doubt.
propositions.quote: In light of the material in the record, and particularly the consistency of the results, there was absolutely no evidence tending to show that the alleged defect cast doubt on the reliability of the results.

propositions.text: Accepting evidence based on speculation is a legal error; the Court did not err in setting aside the acquittal.
propositions.quote: acceptance of theoretical evidence based on speculation reflects a misinterpretation of the accused’s burden of proof, which is an error of law. The Superior Court did not err in setting aside the respondent’s acquittal and ordering a new trial.

paragraphs.summary: No evidence linked the defect to unreliable results; speculation is a legal error, and the Court upheld the order for a new trial.

propositions.quote: An intervener, the Criminal Lawyers’ Association, argues that it would be impossible for an accused to testify about his or her alcohol consumption or digestive problems without contravening s. 258(1) (d.01) Cr. C.

propositions.text: Testifying about health issues like digestion is admissible and does not necessarily violate the law.
propositions.quote: the fact that such testimonial evidence is admissible does not make it compulsory.

paragraphs.summary: Testifying about health issues like digestion is admissible and distinct from challenging instrument operation.

propositions.quote: The burping defence was an essential part of his arguments. He argued that the improper operation of the instrument cast doubt on the reliability of the results precisely because, in such a case, the police might not notice certain digestive issues that can have a distorting effect.

propositions.text: The central issue was whether the defect could affect the results’ reliability.
propositions.quote: the discussion during the hearing before the Court of Québec judge confirms that this question was central to the respondent’s submissions.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent’s main argument was whether digestive issues could impact the reliability of the breath test results.

propositions.text: There was no evidence that the defect affected the results, so the defect could not form the basis of a reasonable doubt.
propositions.quote: In light of the material in the record, and particularly the consistency of the results, there was absolutely no evidence tending to show that the alleged defect cast doubt on the reliability of the results.

propositions.text: Accepting evidence based on speculation is a legal error; the Court did not err in setting aside the acquittal.
propositions.quote: acceptance of theoretical evidence based on speculation reflects a misinterpretation of the accused’s burden of proof, which is an error of law. The Superior Court did not err in setting aside the respondent’s acquittal and ordering a new trial.

paragraphs.summary: No evidence linked the defect to unreliable results; speculation is a legal error, and the Court upheld the order for a new trial.

propositions.text: The Court refers to R. v. St‑Onge Lamoureux, 2012 SCC 57, regarding the right to be presumed innocent and the reliability of breathalyzer results.
propositions.quote: It was held in R. v. St‑Onge Lamoureux, 2012 SCC 57, [2012] 3 S.C.R. 187, at para. 27, that the evidentiary scheme applicable to offences involving driving with a blood alcohol level over the legal limit infringes the right to be presumed innocent guaranteed by s. 11 (d) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

propositions.text: The reliability of the results depends on the proper functioning and operation of the instrument.
propositions.quote: One reason why this infringement is justified in part is because of the recognized reliability of breathalyzer test results. However, the reliability of the results is itself contingent on the proper functioning and proper operation of the instrument.

propositions.text: If an accused raises a reasonable doubt about the instrument’s functioning, the presumption of accuracy must be discarded.
propositions.quote: Where an accused raises a reasonable doubt in this regard, there is no longer any basis for the presumptions of accuracy and identity created by s. 258(1) (c) of the Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C‑46, and those presumptions must be discarded.

paragraphs.summary: The Court discusses the legal framework and the importance of proper instrument functioning for the presumption of test accuracy.

propositions.text: The trial judge found that the technician's testimony raised a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the breathalyzer results.
propositions.quote: the observation period required prior to the administration of the breathalyzer test had not been complied with and that this was sufficient to raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the results

propositions.text: The court upheld the trial judge's decision, emphasizing that it was a matter of weighing evidence.
propositions.quote: the acquittal must therefore be upheld

paragraphs.summary: The court found the trial judge's decision to be correct, based on the technician's testimony raising doubt about reliability.

propositions.text: Requiring evidence that improper operation led to inaccurate results would upset constitutional rights and legislative objectives.
propositions.quote: such a requirement would render even more illusory the defences on which the constitutionality of the evidentiary scheme depends

propositions.text: Recent case law shows breathalyzer records are not available under first-party disclosure.
propositions.quote: breathalyzer maintenance records are not available under first party disclosure

paragraphs.summary: The court notes that requiring proof of inaccurate results would conflict with constitutional rights and recent case law.

propositions.text: The court will discuss the reasoning in St‑Onge Lamoureux and clarify burdens of proof regarding breathalyzer operation.
propositions.quote: I will then discuss this Court’s reasoning in St‑Onge Lamoureux. Then, I will provide some clarification concerning the respective burdens of the defence and the Crown

propositions.text: The court will analyze the case facts to show the original verdict of acquittal was correct.
propositions.quote: I will then consider the facts of this case in order to demonstrate that the original verdict of acquittal is, in my view, unimpeachable

propositions.text: The court will conclude that ordering a new trial would be unfair because the Crown relies on new arguments.
propositions.quote: it would be unfair to order a new trial given the fact that the Crown is relying on arguments made for the first time on appeal

paragraphs.summary: The court outlines its plan to discuss legal reasoning, clarify burdens, analyze facts, and address fairness regarding a new trial.

propositions.text: The appeal involves the burden on an accused to counter presumptions in s. 258(1)(c) of the Criminal Code.
propositions.quote: this appeal requires the Court to consider the burden resting on an accused who seeks to counter the presumptions of accuracy and identity in s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C.

propositions.text: It also concerns the evidence needed to discharge that burden.
propositions.quote: the type of evidence that the accused must adduce to discharge that burden

paragraphs.summary: The appeal addresses the burden and evidence required for an accused to challenge statutory presumptions under s. 258(1)(c).

propositions.text: The court's position is based on the majority in St‑Onge Lamoureux, which acknowledged the relevance of that case.
propositions.quote: My position is based, as it was in the recent decision in Gubbins, on the majority reasons in St‑Onge Lamoureux.

propositions.text: The court notes that St‑Onge Lamoureux upheld the validity of the evidentiary scheme despite some rights infringement.
propositions.quote: the validity of the evidentiary scheme applicable to offences involving driving with a blood alcohol level over the legal limit was upheld in part in St‑Onge Lamoureux, despite the infringement of the right to be presumed innocent

propositions.text: The Court emphasized that the accused could still raise a reasonable doubt about the breathalyzer's operation.
propositions.quote: there was still a real possibility that the accused could counter the statutory presumptions by raising a reasonable doubt about the proper operation of the breathalyzer

paragraphs.summary: The court's view is based on the majority in St‑Onge Lamoureux, which upheld the scheme but allowed for raising doubts about operation.

propositions.text: The scientific evidence shows that improper use of breathalyzers is a real risk, not just speculative.
propositions.quote: the possibility of an instrument malfunctioning or being used improperly when breath samples are taken is not merely speculative, but is very real

propositions.text: Proper operation and maintenance are crucial for accurate results, as per Hodgson’s report.
propositions.quote: to achieve scientifically sound results in operational use, user agencies must ensure that approved instruments are operated by qualified personnel using procedures based on good laboratory practice

paragraphs.summary: Scientific evidence confirms that improper operation of breathalyzers is a real concern, emphasizing the importance of proper procedures.

propositions.text: The Court cited recommendations from the Canadian Society of Forensic Science on procedures before collecting a breath sample.
propositions.quote: The Alcohol Test Committee (“Committee”) of the Canadian Society of Forensic Science (“CSFS”) has made a series of recommendations concerning the procedures to be followed by the professionals who operate the instruments

propositions.text: The recommended observation period before collecting a breath sample is 15 minutes.
propositions.quote: the qualified technician must, among other things, observe the test subject for 15 minutes

propositions.text: These procedures aim to ensure the reliability of the results.
propositions.quote: the purpose is to ensure the reliability of the results

paragraphs.summary: The court references expert recommendations that specify a 15-minute observation to ensure breathalyzer reliability.

propositions.text: The Court emphasized that the constitutionality of the law depends on how easily an accused can rebut the presumption.
propositions.quote: the constitutionality of the provisions at issue depended, among other things, on “whether it is possible, and how easy it is, for the accused to rebut the presumption”

propositions.text: The Court considered whether the accused can show proper procedures were followed.
propositions.quote: whether it is possible, and how easy it is, for the accused to rebut the presumption

paragraphs.summary: The law's constitutionality hinges on the ease with which an accused can rebut the presumption of accuracy.

propositions.text: The Court found that the first of three requirements on the accused—showing malfunction or improper operation—is justified under s. 1 of the Charter.
propositions.quote: only the first of the three requirements imposed on the accused by s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C. — that of adducing evidence tending to show that the instrument was malfunctioning or was operated improperly — constituted a reasonable limit on the right to be presumed innocent

propositions.text: This requirement is justified because proper operation and maintenance are essential for reliable results.
propositions.quote: it reflected the fact that “the results will be reliable only if the instruments are operated and maintained properly”

paragraphs.summary: The court justifies the first requirement on the accused as it ensures the reliability of breathalyzer results, consistent with s. 1 of the Charter.

propositions.text: The Court did not specify the exact evidence needed to show improper operation but noted recommendations from experts.
propositions.quote: The Court declined to specifically determine the nature and scope of the evidence required to show that the instrument was operated improperly

propositions.text: Recommendations from the Canadian Society of Forensic Science suggest mechanisms to ensure proper functioning.
propositions.quote: It can be inferred from these recommendations that the instruments may not function optimally if the suggested procedures are not followed

paragraphs.summary: The Court did not define specific evidence but highlighted expert recommendations for proper breathalyzer operation.

propositions.text: The Court concluded that showing a failure to follow procedures can undermine the presumption's validity.
propositions.quote: it was ultimately in light of the fact that it was possible for the accused to show that the relevant procedures had not been followed — in which case the reliability of the results could not be assumed

propositions.text: This understanding clarifies the burden on the accused to challenge the presumption.
propositions.quote: that the first requirement imposed by s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C. was justified under s. 1 of the Charter

paragraphs.summary: The court clarifies that failure to follow procedures can challenge the presumption, justifying the first requirement under s. 1 of the Charter.

propositions.text: The court states that the case does not require the accused to prove the results are inaccurate, only to raise a doubt about proper operation.
propositions.quote: the accused is not required to show that the results are in fact inaccurate

propositions.text: The statutory conditions are limited to those in s. 258(1)(c)(ii) to (iv).
propositions.quote: The only applicable statutory conditions are those imposed by Parliament in s. 258(1) (c)(ii) to (iv)

paragraphs.summary: The accused need only raise a doubt about proper operation, not prove inaccuracy, within the statutory conditions.

propositions.text: The Court agrees that the burden is to raise a reasonable doubt about the breathalyzer's reliability.
propositions.quote: an accused who seeks to counter the statutory presumptions bears only the burden of adducing evidence tending to show a malfunction or improper operation of the breathalyzer that could affect the reliability of the results

propositions.text: The evidence must only raise a reasonable doubt, not prove malfunction or inaccuracy.
propositions.quote: the evidence in question need only raise a reasonable doubt in this regard

propositions.text: The evidence should show a defect that could cast doubt on the results' reliability.
propositions.quote: evidence of a “defect that could cast doubt on the reliability of the results”

propositions.text: The burden ends when the accused shows a defect affecting reliability, not accuracy.
propositions.quote: The accused’s burden ends there, because the application of the presumptions in s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C. is justified only insofar as the relevant procedures are complied with

paragraphs.summary: The burden on the accused is to show a defect that could affect reliability, not necessarily prove inaccuracy.

propositions.text: Once the accused raises a doubt, the Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the results were unaffected by the defect.
propositions.quote: The burden then shifts to the Crown to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the deficiency in question had no impact on the accuracy of the results on the facts of the case

propositions.text: Failing to do so results in losing the benefit of the presumption.
propositions.quote: if the Crown fails to discharge this burden, it completely loses the benefit of the statutory presumptions in s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C

propositions.text: The Crown cannot rely on technician’s rigour if reliability is challenged.
propositions.quote: The Crown should not be able to rely on the rigour of the technicians to persuade this Court that the results are reliable and then trivialize the importance of that rigour when the reliability of the results is challenged

paragraphs.summary: The Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the defect did not impact the results; otherwise, the presumption is lost.

propositions.text: The accused can rely solely on the technician’s testimony to raise a reasonable doubt.
propositions.quote: There is nothing to prevent the accused from relying solely on the qualified technician’s testimony to raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the results

propositions.text: Technician testimony alone can be sufficient to challenge the presumption.
propositions.quote: evidence to counter the statutory presumptions may be “sought in depositions given by witnesses of the Crown as well as in depositions of defence witnesses”

propositions.text: Technicians responsible for operation can testify about procedures and admit if they did not follow them.
propositions.quote: the qualified technician is responsible for the proper operation of the breathalyzer ... testifies about a recommended procedure, states that its purpose is to ensure the reliability of the results and, finally, admits that he or she did not follow the procedure faithfully or does not know whether it was followed faithfully

propositions.text: Such testimony alone can raise a reasonable doubt about the results’ reliability.
propositions.quote: that the accused is not obliged to tender additional evidence — such as a copy of the training manual in issue — to corroborate the technician’s testimony. That testimony is in itself evidence that can raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the results

paragraphs.summary: Technician testimony alone can be enough for the accused to challenge the presumption of accuracy and reliability.

propositions.text: St-Onge Lamoureux requires evidence that raises a reasonable doubt about the reliability of results, not accuracy.
propositions.quote: St‑Onge Lamoureux requires evidence that raises a reasonable doubt about the reliability rather than the accuracy of the results.

propositions.text: Reliability refers to a system functioning without incident over time, accuracy to conformity to the truth.
propositions.quote: These two terms, though related, do not have the same meaning. The former refers, in its technical sense, to the ability of a system . . . to function without incident for a period of time and, by extension, to the nature of [something that can be relied on]. The latter refers to conformity to the truth.

propositions.text: In St-Onge Lamoureux, accused must raise doubt about reliability, not accuracy, to challenge presumptions.
propositions.quote: Instead, the Court asked the accused to raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the results. In my opinion, this distinction is significant.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the difference between reliability and accuracy, emphasizing that the accused must raise doubt about reliability, not accuracy, per St-Onge Lamoureux.

propositions.text: Evidence showing malfunction or improper operation affects reliability, meeting the burden to raise doubt.
propositions.quote: where the evidence tends to show — on the reasonable doubt standard — that the malfunctioning or improper operation of the breathalyzer increased the possibility of an inaccurate result, then reliability is affected and the accused has met his or her burden.

propositions.text: Proving procedural non-compliance can be enough to raise doubt about reliability.
propositions.quote: In practice, it will be sufficient to adduce evidence tending to show that a recommended procedure was not faithfully followed and that the purpose of the procedure is to ensure the reliability of the results.

propositions.text: Application of s. 258(1)(c) presumption is justified only if procedures are followed.
propositions.quote: the application of the presumptions in s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C. is justified only insofar as the relevant procedures are complied with.

paragraphs.summary: Evidence of procedural defects or malfunction can raise doubt about reliability, affecting the presumption under s. 258(1)(c).

propositions.text: Burden shifts to Crown to prove no impact on accuracy beyond a reasonable doubt.
propositions.quote: The burden then shifts to the Crown to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the deficiency in question had no impact on the accuracy of the results on the facts of the case.

propositions.text: Failing to prove no impact results in loss of statutory presumptions.
propositions.quote: if the Crown fails to discharge this burden, it completely loses the benefit of the statutory presumptions in s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C.

propositions.text: Cyr-Langlois argues Crown cannot rely on technician’s rigour when reliability is challenged.
propositions.quote: [t]he Crown should not be able to rely on the rigour of the technicians to persuade this Court that the results are reliable and then trivialize the importance of that rigour when the reliability of the results is challenged.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown must prove no impact on accuracy beyond a reasonable doubt; failure results in losing presumptions; Crown's reliance on technician’s rigour is challenged.

propositions.text: Accused can rely solely on technician’s testimony to raise doubt about reliability.
propositions.quote: There is nothing to prevent the accused from relying solely on the qualified technician’s testimony to raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the results.

propositions.text: Evidence to counter presumptions can include Crown and defence depositions.
propositions.quote: evidence to counter the statutory presumptions may be “sought in depositions given by witnesses of the Crown as well as in depositions of defence witnesses”.

paragraphs.summary: Accused may rely on technician testimony alone; evidence to challenge presumptions includes depositions from Crown and defence witnesses.

propositions.text: Technician responsible for proper operation; testimony about procedures can raise doubt.
propositions.quote: Where the technician testifies about a recommended procedure, states that its purpose is to ensure the reliability of the results and, finally, admits that he or she did not follow the procedure faithfully or does not know whether it was followed faithfully, the accused is not obliged to tender additional evidence.

propositions.text: Technician’s testimony alone can raise reasonable doubt about results’ reliability.
propositions.quote: That testimony is in itself evidence that can raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the results.

propositions.text: This recognizes the role of qualified technicians in blood alcohol analysis.
propositions.quote: To take the opposite position would be to disregard the unique role conferred by Parliament on qualified technicians in the context of blood alcohol analysis.

paragraphs.summary: Technician’s testimony about procedures can raise doubt; their role in blood alcohol analysis is significant and recognized by law.

propositions.text: The trier of fact assesses evidence to determine if it is enough to rebut statutory presumptions.
propositions.quote: It is for the trier of fact to assess the evidence adduced in order to determine whether it is sufficient to counter the statutory presumptions.

propositions.text: The trier of fact may find that technician’s testimony does not raise a reasonable doubt if problems are trivial or frivolous.
propositions.quote: the qualified technician’s testimony does not in itself raise a reasonable doubt, for example because the problems identified are “frivolous or trivial”.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph states that the trier of fact evaluates evidence to rebut statutory presumptions, including whether technician testimony raises a reasonable doubt.

propositions.text: The trial judge correctly stated the law and supported findings with evidence, leading to an unimpeachable verdict of acquittal.
propositions.quote: The trial judge correctly stated the law. He properly noted that the accused must adduce evidence tending to show that the breathalyzer was malfunctioning or was operated improperly and that the deficiency in question must raise a reasonable doubt about the “reliability of the test taken”. His findings of fact on this point are supported by the evidence adduced by the parties. In my opinion, the verdict of acquittal is therefore unimpeachable.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph affirms the trial judge correctly applied the law and supported his findings with evidence, resulting in an unassailable acquittal.

propositions.text: The Crown did not identify legal errors; the deprivation of presumptions was due to concrete evidence of procedural deficiencies.
propositions.quote: The Crown has not identified any error of law that would warrant this Court’s intervention. Contrary to what it argues, it was deprived of the benefit of the presumptions in s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C. not because of a “mere speculative possibility”, but rather because of concrete and specific evidence showing that a relevant procedure — observation of the accused for a period of time — had not been followed and that this deficiency could affect the reliability of the results.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph states that the Crown's deprivation of presumptions was based on specific procedural evidence, not legal error.

propositions.text: The majority erred in claiming the trial judge misinterpreted the reasonable doubt standard and based findings on speculation.
propositions.quote: I cannot agree with the majority that the trial judge misinterpreted the reasonable doubt standard and that his findings were based on “speculation”.

propositions.text: The reasonable doubt standard relates to improper operation affecting test reliability, not to the accuracy of the blood alcohol level.
propositions.quote: The reasonable doubt simply had to relate to improper operation of the breathalyzer that could affect the reliability of the results.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph criticizes the majority for misinterpreting the reasonable doubt standard and clarifies its scope.

propositions.text: Evidence of improper operation can raise a reasonable doubt about test reliability, a matter for the trier of fact.
propositions.quote: evidence of improper operation may in itself raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the results.

propositions.text: Assessing the sufficiency of such evidence is a matter for the trier of fact, citing relevant case law.
propositions.quote: since it involves assessing the sufficiency of the evidence (see Sunbeam Corporation (Canada) Ltd. v. The Queen, [1969] S.C.R. 221, at p. 231; Lampard v. The Queen, [1969] S.C.R. 373, at pp. 380‑81; Schuldt v. The Queen, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 592, at p. 608).

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph states that evidence of improper operation can raise reasonable doubt, and its sufficiency is for the trier of fact to decide.

propositions.text: The evidence about improper operation was sufficient to raise a reasonable doubt, so the Court should not intervene.
propositions.quote: the trial judge found that that evidence was sufficient to raise a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the results. This Court should therefore not intervene.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph concludes that the evidence was enough to create reasonable doubt, warranting no intervention by the Court.

propositions.text: Constable Boissonneault testified that a 20-minute observation period is required to ensure no residual alcohol affects results.
propositions.quote: Constable Boissonneault, the qualified technician, himself stated that the procedures prescribed by the École nationale de police du Québec include a 20‑minute observation period.

propositions.text: This procedure aims to prevent residual mouth alcohol from distorting breathalyzer results, and no additional evidence was needed to establish its existence.
propositions.quote: This testimony was more than sufficient to show that a procedure exists for ensuring the reliability of the test results. There was no need to file the training manual of the École nationale de police du Québec, to which the witness referred, or to have an expert testify to corroborate what the witness had said.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph details the technician’s testimony about the observation period to ensure test reliability, which was sufficient evidence.

propositions.text: Constable Boissonneault did not observe the accused during the entire period; another officer did, but not continuously.
propositions.quote: Constable Boissonneault stated that he had not observed the accused himself because he had been busy preparing the breathalyzer. Another police officer, Constable Cousineau, did so instead.

propositions.text: Constable Cousineau could not confirm continuous observation, and some time was unobserved due to the accused exercising his right to counsel.
propositions.quote: there was a certain amount of time during which Constable Cousineau was unable to determine whether Mr. Cyr‑Langlois burped, since Mr. Cyr‑Langlois was alone in a soundproof room exercising his right to counsel.

propositions.text: The technician’s failure to ensure continuous observation could lead the trial judge to doubt procedural compliance.
propositions.quote: the trial judge could certainly find that the qualified technician’s testimony was sufficient to raise a reasonable doubt about compliance with the prescribed observation period.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph discusses the lack of continuous observation and its implications for procedural compliance and reliability.

propositions.text: The trial judge could reasonably find that the technician’s failure to follow procedures raised doubt about test reliability.
propositions.quote: the qualified technician administered the tests without faithfully following the prescribed procedure and without ensuring, as he was required to do, that the accused did not have any physiological reaction that could distort the results.

propositions.text: This evidence was sufficient to create a reasonable doubt about the reliability of the breathalyzer results.
propositions.quote: the trial judge could therefore have a reasonable doubt about their reliability.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph states that the technician’s procedural lapses could reasonably lead to doubt about test reliability.

propositions.text: The accused discharged his burden under s. 258(1)(c) Cr. C., so no further evidence was needed.
propositions.quote: At that point, the accused had discharged his burden under s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C. and did not have to adduce any other evidence.

propositions.text: The judge need not extend the presumption if the evidence shows the possibility of invalid results, as per Hogue J.A.
propositions.quote: In the absence of additional evidence allowing him to conclude that the possibility of the invalid result to which Officer Boissonneault referred could be ruled out, the first instance judge was entitled not to extend the benefit of the presumptions to the prosecution.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph explains that the accused met his burden, and the judge was justified in not applying the presumption further.

propositions.text: Requiring the accused to testify about physiological reactions infringes rights, as the state must ensure procedural compliance.
propositions.quote: it would be contrary to the right to remain silent and the right to be presumed innocent to require an accused to testify about his or her alcohol consumption and physiological reactions.

propositions.text: The majority’s approach improperly shifts the burden to the accused, which could unjustifiably infringe rights.
propositions.quote: the majority’s approach shifts the obligation to the accused to observe himself or herself, make note of every physiological reaction and then testify about this, failing which the improper operation of the breathalyzer will be presumed to be of no consequence.

propositions.text: It is the state’s responsibility to ensure procedural compliance, not the accused’s.
propositions.quote: It is the state’s responsibility, not that of the accused, to ensure that no physiological reactions occurred before he took the breath samples.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph discusses the rights of the accused and the state’s obligation to ensure procedural accuracy without infringing rights.

propositions.text: The Crown failed to prove that non-compliance with observation procedures affected the results, so presumptions could not be justified.
propositions.quote: the onus was on the Crown to prove it, for example by having the qualified technician or an expert testify on this point. The Crown did not do so, however, and it must accept the consequences.

propositions.text: Failure to prove that procedural non-compliance affected results means the presumptions of accuracy and identity cannot be justified.
propositions.quote: the application of the presumptions of accuracy and identity in s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C. was no longer justified, and the presumptions therefore had to be discarded.

propositions.text: Without evidence of guilt, the trial judge had no choice but to acquit.
propositions.quote: the trial judge had no choice but to acquit him.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph states that the Crown did not prove procedural non-compliance affected results, invalidating the presumptions and leading to acquittal.

propositions.text: Even if the Crown’s new argument about evidence was accepted, a new trial would be inappropriate.
propositions.quote: even if I agreed with the Crown’s position that the accused had to introduce the qualified technician’s training manual in evidence and to testify about his alcohol consumption and physiological reactions, I would hesitate to order a new trial in this case.

propositions.text: The Crown’s position on appeal differed from its position at trial, which is relevant to the appropriateness of a new trial.
propositions.quote: the position taken by the prosecution on appeal is clearly different from the one it took at trial.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph suggests that ordering a new trial would be inappropriate due to the Crown’s changed position and the risk of double jeopardy.

propositions.text: The Crown did not argue at trial that the technician’s testimony was insufficient or that manuals or testimony about alcohol consumption were necessary.
propositions.quote: Most importantly, he did not argue that the accused had to testify about his alcohol consumption and physiological reactions (such as burping) because otherwise there could be no reasonable doubt about the reliability of the results.

propositions.text: The Crown’s actual trial position was that observation was sufficient, not that additional evidence was required.
propositions.quote: the prosecutor’s position was that Constables Boissonneault and Cousineau had observed the accused for a period of time that was sufficient in the circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph notes that the Crown’s original trial position did not include requiring additional evidence or testimony about alcohol consumption.

propositions.text: Ordering a new trial would give the Crown a second chance based on arguments made only on appeal, violating double jeopardy.
propositions.quote: To order a new trial would therefore be to give the Crown a second chance to have Mr. Cyr‑Langlois convicted, on the basis of arguments that were made for the first time on appeal.

propositions.text: Such a second chance would violate the principle against double jeopardy.
propositions.quote: In my view, such a result would be contrary to the double jeopardy principle.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph argues that a new trial based on new arguments on appeal would breach double jeopardy principles.

propositions.text: The trial judge’s decision was correct in finding that the evidence raised a reasonable doubt about test operation.
propositions.quote: In summary, the trial judge made no reviewable error in finding that Mr. Cyr‑Langlois had raised a reasonable doubt about improper operation of the breathalyzer that could affect the results and that the presumptions of accuracy and identity in s. 258(1) (c) Cr. C. had therefore been countered.

propositions.text: The trial judge did not need to require further evidence from the accused.
propositions.quote: I agree with Hogue J.A. that the trial judge [translation] “did not have to require anything further from the accused”

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph affirms that the trial judge correctly found a reasonable doubt and was not required to seek additional evidence.

propositions.text: The majority’s approach unduly limits defenses based on improper breathalyzer operation, affecting the statutory scheme and Charter rights.
propositions.quote: In my view, the majority’s approach unduly limits the defences based on improper operation of a breathalyzer that in fact make it possible to justify the evidentiary scheme applicable to offences involving driving with a blood alcohol level over the legal limit under s. 1 of the Charter.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph criticizes the majority for restricting defenses related to improper breathalyzer operation, impacting legal and Charter protections.

propositions.text: The majority’s reasons are based on arguments the Crown made only on appeal, making a new trial inappropriate.
propositions.quote: Finally, the majority’s reasons are essentially based on arguments that the Crown made for the first time on appeal. It would be all the more inappropriate, in the circumstances, to order a new trial.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph states that the majority’s reasoning relies on arguments raised only on appeal, making a new trial unjustified.

propositions.text: The appeal should be dismissed; the Court allows the Crown’s appeal, with Côté J. dissenting.
propositions.quote: For all these reasons, I would dismiss the appeal. Appeal allowed, Côté J. dissenting.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph concludes that the appeal should be dismissed, with a dissenting opinion from Côté J.
